title: Historic Paint Colors for Gainesville Homes
description: Choosing period-appropriate exterior colors for older Gainesville homes: matching the era, body-trim-accent schemes, district review, and lead-safe prep.
excerpt: How to choose period-appropriate exterior colors for an older Gainesville home, from era and scheme to district review and lead-safe prep.
h1: Historic Paint Colors for Gainesville Homes
heroIntro: Gainesville’s older neighborhoods, from the Duckpond area to the streets around downtown and the university, hold bungalows, Victorians, and Folk Victorian cottages that look their best in colors chosen for their era. Here is how to get it right.

questions: How do I choose historic paint colors for my house?
Do I need approval to paint a house in a Gainesville historic district?
What colors were used on Victorian and bungalow homes?

sections.h2: Match the era and style of the house
body: Historic color is less about finding one "correct" shade and more about matching the logic of the period the house was built in. Paint technology, pigment availability, and taste changed dramatically from the late 1800s through the mid-1900s, and each style carries its own conventions. Before looking at chips, pin down roughly when your house was built and which style family it belongs to. County property records, the original architectural details, and neighborhood histories are good starting points. Here is how the styles most common in Gainesville were traditionally colored.
bullets: Victorian and Queen Anne: often multi-color schemes, with a body color, a contrasting trim color, and one or two accent colors picking out brackets, spindles, and window sashes. Deeper earth tones and rich greens, reds, and golds were typical in the later Victorian period.
Folk Victorian and frame vernacular: simpler, frequently light body colors such as whites, creams, and pale grays or yellows, with contrasting trim and darker shutters or doors.
Craftsman bungalows: earthy, nature-based palettes like olive, sage, brown, ochre, and muted reds, with trim that often contrasts in a cream or a darker shade, and stained or deep-colored doors.
Colonial Revival: light body colors, especially white, cream, pale yellow, and soft gray, with white trim and dark green or black shutters.
Mid-century homes: a wider range, including soft pastels and clean contrasts, often with simple trim.

body: Most traditional exteriors use a body, trim, and accent structure. The body is the largest field of siding. Trim covers corner boards, window and door casings, fascia, and porch elements. Accents are reserved for doors, sashes, shutters, and small decorative details. Getting the proportions right matters more than any single color. A common mistake on older houses is painting everything one color and losing the architectural detail, or the opposite, using too many accents on a modest cottage.

Sheen follows the same logic. Keep the body in a flat or low-sheen finish, use satin on trim, and save higher gloss for doors, shutters, and railings, which is both historically appropriate and practical because those surfaces get handled.

If you want to know what your house actually looked like, the clues are often still on it. Carefully scraping a small, protected area, such as behind a shutter, under a porch ceiling, or on the back of a trim piece, can reveal paint layers. A sharp blade cut at a shallow angle through the layers (a "crater" or "cross-section") lets you see the sequence. Remember that old paint has faded and yellowed with age, so match to the least-exposed sample, not the weathered surface.
Old photographs from family, previous owners, or local archives help too, even in black and white, since they show contrast between body and trim.
Before you scrape anything, read the next section.

sections.h2: Lead paint is almost certain on historic homes
body: Houses built before 1978 are very likely to have lead-based paint somewhere on the exterior, and on homes from the early 1900s it is close to a given. Test before sanding or scraping. If lead is present, use lead-safe work practices: plastic sheeting on the ground, wet scraping instead of dry sanding, no open-flame burning or high-heat stripping, careful debris cleanup, and keeping children and pets away. Paid renovation work on pre-1978 homes must follow the EPA Renovation, Repair and Painting rule, so ask any contractor how they handle it.

sections.h2: Check district guidance before you buy paint
body: Gainesville has locally designated historic districts and individually listed properties, and exterior changes in those areas can be subject to review. Requirements differ by district and by what you are changing, so contact the City of Gainesville’s historic preservation staff to confirm whether your property is in a district and whether your project, including color, needs approval. If you are in a homeowners association, check its rules as well. Verifying first avoids repainting a wall you have already finished.

sections.h2: Adapting period colors to Florida sun
body: Some traditional colors behave differently under our UV than they would in a northern town. Deep reds, saturated greens, and dark blues on large body areas fade faster and run hotter on sunny walls, which adds stress to old wood. One practical approach is to keep the body in a lighter or mid-tone period color and let the deeper, historically rich colors live on the accents, doors, and sashes, where they are easier to refresh.

Light can also wash out subtle period tones. A soft historic gray-green that looks perfect on a chip may read almost white on a sunny south wall. Paint large samples on the actual siding, on more than one side of the house, and look at them in morning and afternoon light before deciding. Ask for the best-quality exterior line you can, since pigment quality affects how well a color holds up.

sections.h2: Protecting old wood in our climate
body: Historic wood siding is often old-growth lumber that is denser and more stable than modern boards, and it is worth preserving. It does need careful prep: scraping to a sound edge, consolidating and filling soft spots or replacing damaged pieces in kind, priming bare wood with a quality exterior primer, and caulking only the joints that should be sealed. Avoid high-pressure washing on old wood; a gentle wash is safer. Good ventilation behind the siding and clear gutters go a long way, and our article on hidden moisture behind siding covers what to watch for.
For interiors in older homes, see our guide to interior colors that work with Florida light.

faqs.q: Do I need approval to paint my house in a Gainesville historic district?
faqs.a: It depends on the district and the scope of the change. Contact the City of Gainesville’s historic preservation staff before you start to confirm what review, if any, applies to your property and project.

faqs.q: How do I find my house’s original paint color?
faqs.a: Look for layers in protected areas like behind shutters or under porch ceilings, and check old photos. Test for lead before scraping, and match to the least-faded sample.

faqs.q: What colors suit a Craftsman bungalow?
faqs.a: Earthy, nature-inspired colors such as olive, sage, brown, ochre, and muted reds are traditional, typically with contrasting trim and a stained or deep-colored front door.

faqs.q: Is lead paint a concern on historic homes?
faqs.a: Yes. Homes built before 1978 often have lead paint. Test before disturbing it, and use lead-safe practices or a contractor who follows the EPA RRP rule.
